summary: San Francisco's annual average high of just 60°F makes it one of the coldest major cities in the continental U.S. during summer — a fact that surprises nearly everyone who hasn't stood in shorts on the Golden Gate Bridge in July, shivering in 55-degree fog while inland California bakes at 100. That marine layer is the defining weather reality: 8.2 hours of daily sunshine sounds generous until you realize much of it arrives after the fog burns off at noon, and evening walks near Ocean Beach or through Golden Gate Park often require a jacket year-round. The city is genuinely walkable in a way few American cities manage — 47 hills crammed into a tight, roughly seven-by-seven-mile peninsula, with transit running through dense corridors and commercial streets stacked with independent coffee shops, bakeries, and sit-down restaurants at a frequency that rewards exploration on foot. That density comes at a staggering cost: a median home value near $1.38 million against a median household income of roughly $141,000 yields a price-to-income ratio around 9.8, meaning even well-above-median earners face a steep arithmetic wall when attempting to buy. Renting at $2,419 per month is more accessible but still commands roughly 20 percent of gross median income. The job market is anchored by major tech firms, biotech, healthcare systems, and financial services, meaning employment options are abundant without leaving city limits — though property crime rates, particularly larceny at 3,830 per 100,000 and motor vehicle theft at 793, rank well above national averages and shape daily decisions around car ownership and package delivery. San Francisco is a city where the spectacular physical setting — bay panoramas, Pacific coastline, ridgeline sunsets visible from dozens of streets — coexists with a cost structure that makes the math work very differently depending on which side of that 9.8 ratio you land on.
